## What Is an[Employer of Record](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-definition-employer-of-record) in Iceland


An Employer of Record (EOR) is a third-party organization that becomes the legal employer for your team members in Iceland, even though you continue directing their day-to-day work. Instead of registering your own einkahlutafélag (ehf.) and handling Icelandic labor law, tax registration with Skatturinn, and mandatory pension contributions on your own, the EOR takes on that legal and administrative burden. This matters in Iceland because the country’s small population and tightly controlled labor market make entity setup a heavy lift when you’re only hiring one or two people. The EOR signs the employment contract, runs local payroll, withholds and remits taxes, and administers statutory benefits like paid vacation and pension contributions on your behalf. You keep control over the employee’s role, performance, and daily responsibilities, while the EOR generally handles compliance under Icelandic employment law. For most companies testing the Icelandic market or hiring a handful of people, this is the fastest and lowest-risk way in without committing to a local entity.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Iceland


Before you draft your first Icelandic employment contract, it helps to know the compliance environment you’re stepping into. Iceland’s labor market runs on a mix of statutory law and union-driven collective bargaining agreements, and both shape what you owe employees on pay, hours, leave, and termination notice, so getting familiar with the basics upfront can save you from costly missteps later.


Hiring in Iceland means working within a labor market shaped heavily by union influence and collective bargaining agreements (CBAs), which often set minimum wages, working hours, and termination terms beyond what the underlying labor code requires, and can apply by industry even if you never negotiated them directly. Employers generally[register employees with Skatturinn](https://www.skatturinn.is/english/) for income tax withholding, and separately enroll them in[mandatory pension fund contributions](https://www.government.is/publications/legislation/act/2001-07-27-The-Pension-Act-No.-129-1997) through the relevant pension fund, which typically split between employer and employee and run well above what US employers are used to with a 401(k). Icelandic law generally ties notice periods to tenure, and even a termination that feels straightforward can create disputes if the required procedural steps aren’t followed. Employees are typically entitled to statutory paid vacation, public holidays, and parental leave protections that exceed US baselines, and getting these calculations right is part of staying compliant. Because CBA terms can override company-level agreements, it’s worth confirming which agreement applies to your hire before finalizing a contract. This is general information, not legal advice: Iceland’s employment rules vary by sector and change over time, so consult a qualified employment lawyer for your specific situation.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Iceland: Which Is Right for You


You’ve now seen what an EOR costs, what it covers, and what standing up your own ehf. actually involves. The last step is weighing those two paths against each other directly, since an EOR and a local entity solve the same problem of hiring someone in Iceland in very different ways, with different tradeoffs on speed, cost, and control. Here’s how to think through which one fits your situation.


The right choice comes down to timeline, headcount, and how much control you need over benefits and equity. An EOR gets you hiring someone in Iceland in days, with low upfront commitment and reduced misclassification risk, since Bolto’s local entity handles payroll, taxes, pension contributions, and CBA compliance on your behalf. A local ehf. makes more sense once you have enough employees that the fixed legal, accounting, and banking overhead is spread thin, and you want full control over benefits design, equity administration, and direct IP ownership. The tradeoff is that an ehf. takes weeks to months to register and carries ongoing compliance obligations that don’t shrink for a small team, while an EOR keeps you somewhat dependent on a vendor and offers less customization on benefits and equity than you’d get running your own entity. If you’re testing the Icelandic market or hiring your first few people, an EOR is generally the lower-risk, faster path. If you already know you’re building a larger, long-term team there, setting up your own entity can pay off over time despite the upfront lift.
